Name: Akiflow
Vendor: Akiflow Inc., a Delaware corporation with a fully remote team ‘designed in Italy’; Y Combinator lists it in Spain. Privately held, backed by Y Combinator and Benson Oak Ventures.
Market_Evidence: No user or revenue figures are published; Y Combinator lists a team of 18 and the About page shows 12 people (both checked November 2026).
Price_Note: Pro, per person per month billed annually ($228 a year); $34 billed monthly. The annual card has carried a PROMO label since at least November 2025, but no other annual price is published and the FAQ quotes $19 without qualification. Local purchasing-power pricing may apply at checkout.
Free_Plan_Note: No free plan: a 7-day full-access trial that needs a card and converts to a paid subscription unless cancelled.
Plans: One plan, Pro: $34 a month billed monthly or $228 a year ($19 a month) billed annually; the AI Meeting Assistant is a $19-a-month add-on, and team pricing is by quote.
Integrations_Note: 19 native connectors including Google, Outlook and iCloud calendars, Gmail, Outlook mail, Slack, Teams, Notion, Asana, ClickUp, Jira, Linear, GitHub, Trello, Todoist and Microsoft To Do, plus Zapier and IFTTT. No public REST API; an OAuth MCP server gives AI assistants read-write access.
Hosting: Google Cloud Platform, region not stated; no region choice and no self-managed edition. The company participates in the EU-US, UK and Swiss-US Data Privacy Frameworks.
Security: TLS in transit and AES-256 at rest. The vendor states it holds no SOC 2, ISO 27001 or FERPA certification. No SSO, SCIM or audit log.
Calendar_Sync: Two-way event sync with Google Calendar, Outlook Calendar and iCloud Calendar on Pro: events can be created, edited and deleted in Akiflow; iCloud sync is periodic.
Data_Out: No documented export or backup feature; support has pointed users to a SQLite export from a debug settings page. No public REST API; an OAuth 2.1 MCP server can read and write tasks, subtasks and events.
Platforms: Web, macOS, Windows, iOS, Android, Apple Watch and Wear OS. No Linux app.
AI: Aki, a chat and voice assistant in the app and on WhatsApp, plus auto-scheduling and AI project assignment, all included in Pro; the AI Meeting Assistant is a $19 monthly add-on. AI features are opt-in under a Privacy Policy Addendum for AI Features: content is not used to train or fine-tune general-purpose models beyond your organisation, but may be processed to debug and improve Akiflow’s AI and to personalise it. No model provider is named, and none appears in the sub-processor list.
Value_for_money_Review: No free plan, a card for the trial, and $34 a month monthly or a promotional $19 annually for one person.
Ease_of_use_Review: Keyboard-first inbox and drag-to-calendar planning are quick to learn, but connecting and triaging many sources takes setup.
Enterprise_features_Review: No certifications, no SSO or admin console; team pricing is by quote but adds little beyond availability sharing.
Interface_flexibility_Review: Lists, calendar, projects, tags and an AI assistant, but no board, custom fields or automation rules.
Data_control_Review: Google Cloud hosting in an unnamed region and no SOC 2 or ISO 27001, though certified under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework.
Portability_Review: No export feature or public API; support points to a SQLite dump from a debug page, and backups are off the roadmap.
Summary: Akiflow is a planner for individuals who juggle tasks arriving from many places. It collects them into one inbox and asks you to time-block them onto your calendar, and it is sold mainly to founders, executives and other heavy schedulers. Tasks arrive from Gmail, Slack, Notion, Jira, Asana, Linear and about a dozen other tools, then move to Today, Upcoming or a project, and onto the calendar as blocks. An AI assistant, Aki, answers in the app and on WhatsApp, plans days and reads meeting transcripts. There are no boards, Gantt or custom fields, and team features stop at shared availability. There is one plan, Pro, at $34 a month monthly or $19 a month on an annual plan the vendor has labelled a promotion for a year. The trial lasts seven days and needs a card, and the AI Meeting Assistant costs $19 a month more. That makes it one of the dearest single-user tools here. Data sits on Google Cloud in a region the vendor does not name, and Akiflow states it holds no SOC 2 or ISO 27001. There is no export button or public API, and in November 2025 support said backup and export were not on the roadmap. An OAuth MCP server is the only official programmatic route, so leaving is hard. AI features are opt-in, and an addendum says content does not train general-purpose models but may be used to debug and improve Akiflow’s own AI.
Caveat: The $19 annual rate is labelled a promotion and could revert without notice, though the label has stood since at least November 2025. The AI addendum lets Akiflow use AI inputs to improve its own features, and the model provider is not disclosed.

Name: Businessmap
Vendor: Businessmap (formerly Kanbanize). Privately held and founder-led; offices in Sofia, Bulgaria, Bilbao, Spain and São Paulo, Brazil.
Market_Evidence: Businessmap says it is trusted by 1,000+ enterprise PMO and portfolio teams and lists 300+ partners and offices in three countries (businessmap.io, November 2026); it publishes no user or revenue figures.
Price_Note: Standard, per user per month billed annually at the 15-user entry tier ($1,896 a year); $12.70 billed monthly; the rate falls to $8.50 annually at 100 users.
Free_Plan_Note: No free plan; a free trial with full features, including analytics, is offered instead.
Plans: Standard (all features) from $10.60 per user per month annually or $12.70 monthly, sold from 15 seats; automation rules and SSO are paid add-ons; Enterprise is quote-only, adding a dedicated cloud instance, IP whitelisting, 1 TB storage and a customer success manager.
Integrations_Note: Native integrations listed for Jira, GitLab, Bitbucket, Subversion, Power BI, Tableau, Looker Studio, Okta, Entra ID, OneLogin, Excel and Google Sheets add-ins, plus Zapier, Make and Power Automate; a REST API and a remote MCP server.
Hosting: AWS: US (Virginia) by default for the Americas, Ireland or Frankfurt for EU customers; dedicated infrastructure (optional at 500 to 1,000 users, mandatory above 1,000) can be placed in Germany, Spain, São Paulo, Sydney and other regions on request. No self-managed edition.
Security: ISO 27001:2022 and PCI-DSS compliance stated, twice-yearly third-party audits including penetration tests, TLS 1.2 in transit and AES-256 at rest. SAML and OIDC SSO with Okta, Entra ID or OneLogin as a paid add-on; audit logs and admin roles; IP whitelisting on Enterprise. No SOC 2 report was found.
Calendar_Sync: None native. The built-in calendar shows card deadlines and other dates inside Businessmap only; sync with external calendars needs Zapier, Make or Power Automate.
Data_Out: Advanced search results export to Excel with configurable fields, links and subtasks; dashboard widgets export their data; Excel and Google Sheets add-ins import and export cards. REST API (with call limits on Standard) and a remote MCP server. Import is via spreadsheet templates; Enterprise includes free migration from other tools.
Platforms: Web, plus iOS and Android apps listed as “Businessmap formerly Kanbanize” (App Store and Google Play, both last updated in January 2026).
AI: AI Tools generate subtasks, comments, emails and summaries on cards; the AI Coach analyses workflow and card data; whiteboards add AI insights; included in the plan and switchable by an administrator. The privacy policy (updated 6 November 2026) says request content goes to Microsoft Azure OpenAI Service in Sweden or to AWS in the organisation’s data centre, and that neither Businessmap nor its AI providers use it to train models. A remote MCP server lets Claude, ChatGPT and other clients query the account.
Value_for_money_Review: No free plan, a 15-seat entry at $10.60 a seat, and automation rules and SSO both billed as add-ons.
Ease_of_use_Review: Workflows, lanes, initiatives and WIP policies assume Kanban knowledge; most rollouts lean on training or the vendor’s consultants.
Enterprise_features_Review: SAML and OIDC SSO as an add-on, audit logs, granular roles, ISO 27001:2022 and dedicated infrastructure above 500 users.
Interface_flexibility_Review: Boards, portfolio workspaces, Gantt planning view, calendar, OKRs, whiteboards, dashboards, flow analytics and IF-THEN business rules.
Data_control_Review: EU (Dublin, Frankfurt) or US hosting on shared plans, with dedicated AWS instances in other regions on request.
Portability_Review: Search results export to Excel and add-ins sync with Excel or Sheets, but there is no full-account JSON export.
Summary: Businessmap, called Kanbanize until 2023, grew from Kanban boards into a portfolio management platform that links OKRs and initiatives to the cards teams move each day. It is sold mainly to mid-sized and large organisations running Lean or Agile at scale. Work lives on configurable Kanban boards inside workspaces, with initiatives above them on a Gantt-style planning view that supports predecessor links, critical path and milestones. A calendar shows deadlines, cards carry logged time with worklog reports, and flow metrics such as cycle time and blocked time are built in. Business rules automate moves and updates. There is one feature-complete Standard plan and no free tier. It starts at 15 seats: $10.60 per user annually ($12.70 monthly), falling with volume. Automation rules and SSO cost extra, and Enterprise adds dedicated hosting and support. Shared accounts are hosted on AWS in the US or the EU, with dedicated instances in other regions for large customers, and Businessmap states ISO 27001:2022 compliance. AI tools draft subtasks, comments and summaries through Azure OpenAI in Sweden or AWS, and the November 2026 privacy policy says this content is not used to train models. Data leaves through Excel exports and the REST API.
Caveat: Prices come from the vendor’s live pricing calculator, which starts at 15 seats; there is no free plan, and automation rules and SSO add to the per-seat price.

Name: Celoxis

Free_Plan_Note: No free plan; a 14-day trial runs on the Business feature set, and paid plans add free client users plus 2 (Core) to 15 (Business) free read-only users.
Plans: Core $10, Essentials $25, Professional $35 and Business $45 per full-access user per month billed annually, with cheaper team-member and timesheet-only seats from Essentials; Enterprise (including on-premise) is quoted.
Integrations_Note: 21 integrations are configured inside Celoxis, including two-way Jira and Azure DevOps sync, Salesforce, QuickBooks Online, Slack, Okta and MS Project; Zapier and n8n cover the rest, beside a REST API, webhooks and a beta MCP server.
Hosting: Celoxis Cloud on AWS in the United States (default) or Ireland (EU), chosen at sign-up. Security: ISO 27001 and AICPA SOC 2 Type II audited; EU and UK GDPR. SAML 2.0 SSO tested with Google, Salesforce, Okta, OneLogin, Azure and ADFS, with no plan stated; an undefined “Advanced security” item is listed only on Business and Enterprise. Two-factor authentication (in beta); role-based privileges; request logging and an activity log report. Encrypted snapshots every 30 minutes. No SCIM or customer-managed keys documented.

Imports from MS Project (keeping dependencies and constraints) and CSV for tasks, users, clients and time. REST API reads and writes projects, tasks, time, expenses and custom fields, rate-limited from 150 requests an hour on Core to 1,800 on Enterprise; webhooks. On-premise customers hold the database.
Platforms: Web; iOS and Android apps for task updates, time logging and approvals.
AI: Lex, a natural-language assistant over live account data, not listed as a paid item on the pricing page; Microsoft Azure AI Services is the only listed AI provider. Value_for_money_Review: Core is $10 with capacity planning, but a five-seat minimum applies and timesheets add $5 or need Essentials at $25.
Ease_of_use_Review: A scheduling engine with constraints, work calendars and role-based privileges needs a trained administrator to set up.
Enterprise_features_Review: SAML SSO, roles and privileges, activity logs, portfolios and SOC 2 Type II, though no SCIM is documented.
Interface_flexibility_Review: Gantt, card, calendar and chart outputs on any report, dashboards, formula fields and custom workflow apps.
Data_control_Review: A self-hosted edition on Linux, Windows or macOS, plus a choice of US or EU cloud on AWS.
Portability_Review: Gantt and reports export to CSV and MS Project plans import intact, but there is no full workspace export.
Summary: Celoxis is a project portfolio management system that has been sold since 2001, built in Pune for PMOs that run scheduled projects alongside resource capacity, budgets and billing. Its buyers are manufacturing, technology, healthcare and services firms rather than small teams. Plans are task hierarchies with all four dependency types, constraints, baselines and critical path. Every report can be shown as a table, Gantt, calendar, card board with draggable lanes or chart, and dashboards are built from those reports. Timesheets with timers and approvals, expenses, risks and issues and custom workflow apps sit beside the projects. Scrum is handled by convention, with sprints as summary tasks, rather than as a dedicated mode. Core costs $10 per full-access user per month billed annually, with a five-user minimum, and already includes workload tracking and capacity planning; timesheets cost $5 more on Core or come with Essentials at $25, which adds job roles and resource-conflict checks. Project billing, the client portal and an undefined “advanced security” bundle need Business at $45. Enterprise, which includes the on-premise licence, is quoted. The cloud runs on AWS with a choice of US or Ireland data centres, under ISO 27001 and SOC 2 Type II, and a self-hosted edition runs on PostgreSQL, SQL Server or Oracle. The Lex assistant uses Microsoft Azure AI Services and is not priced separately. Exports are CSV and PDF; the REST API and webhooks are the fuller route out.
Caveat: The plan line-up (Core to Business) is new enough that third-party comparisons still quote older tiers; and the five-user minimum means the real entry price is $50 a month, billed annually.

Name: Favro
Vendor: Uppsala collaborative technologies AB, trading as Favro. Privately held, registered in Uppsala, Sweden; founded by Hans Dahlström, Erik Olofsson and Patric Palm, whose earlier agile-planning company was sold to a US acquirer.
Market_Evidence: Favro publishes no user, customer or revenue figures (checked November 2026); its site points to game-development, SaaS and enterprise teams, and its App Store listing carries 12 ratings.
Price_Note: Lite, per user per month billed annually; $6 billed monthly. Sold in team-size buckets of 2, 5, 10, 25, 50 and 100 users, so a 3-person team pays for 5.
Free_Plan_Note: No free plan; every paid plan has a 14-day trial without a card.
Plans: Lite $5.10 per user per month annually ($6 monthly); Standard $6.80 annually ($8 monthly); Enterprise tailored pricing via sales. Minimum bucket is 2 users.
Integrations_Note: About 15 named integrations: Slack, Jira (with an on-premise proxy), GitHub, GitLab, Miro, Google Drive, OneDrive, Google and Outlook calendars, Zapier, Unito, Okta and OneLogin, plus an official MCP server since September 2026. API and webhooks on Standard and Enterprise only; Lite gets only primary integrations.
Hosting: EU only: AWS in Frankfurt and Cleura (City Network) in Frankfurt and Sweden, with attachments in AWS S3. No region choice today; Favro says an Enterprise Plus plan will add it. No self-managed edition.
Security: ISO/IEC 27001 and 27701 certified by a third party; PCI DSS SAQ A. TLS 1.2+ in transit, database and backups encrypted at rest. Google and GitHub OAuth on all plans; SAML SSO (Okta, OneLogin) and SCIM 1.0/2.0 on Enterprise. No audit log published.
Calendar_Sync: Each member can connect Google or Microsoft calendar so start and due dates of cards assigned to them appear there; one way, and only for cards assigned after connecting. A built-in calendar shows dated cards across collections.
Data_Out: Board export to Excel, CSV or JSON from sheet view; whether comments and attachments are included is not documented. The REST API reads cards, comments, custom fields and dependencies. Importers for Trello, Basecamp Classic and CSV or Excel. API and webhooks on Standard (1,000 calls an hour) and Enterprise (10,000).
Platforms: Web, iOS, Android, and desktop apps for macOS and Windows.
AI: No built-in AI features and no AI fees. An official MCP server (since September 2026) lets external assistants such as Claude, ChatGPT and Cursor act with the user’s own permissions; data handling then follows those assistants’ terms.
Value_for_money_Review: Cheap at $5.10 Lite, but no free plan, 2-user buckets, and Lite drops integrations, the API and reports.
Ease_of_use_Review: Cards that live on several boards at once are flexible but take a team time to model well.
Enterprise_features_Review: Enterprise adds SAML SSO, SCIM provisioning, collection management and timesheets; no audit log or portfolio layer is advertised.
Interface_flexibility_Review: Boards, sheets, roadmaps, backlogs, calendar, dashboards, documents, forms, relations and 5,000 monthly automations on Standard.
Data_control_Review: ISO 27001 and 27701 certified with data held in the EU (Frankfurt and Sweden); no region choice yet.
Portability_Review: Boards export to Excel, CSV or JSON from sheet view, but the API is closed to Lite customers.
Summary: Favro is a Swedish planning tool built by the founders of an earlier enterprise agile product. It is sold to teams that run several boards in parallel, especially game studios and software companies, and to managers who need to see across them. Its distinctive idea is that one card can live on several boards at once, so a task appears on a team’s Kanban board, a manager’s sheet and a roadmap without copying. Collections group boards; backlogs nest cards into hierarchies; relations, dependencies, burndowns, dashboards, forms, documents and a calendar sit on top, and rule-based automations move work along. There is no free plan. Lite at $5.10 a user is limited to five collections, 25 automation actions a month and no integrations or API, so most teams will need Standard at $6.80. Users are billed in buckets from two seats, and timesheets, SAML SSO and SCIM are Enterprise only. Data stays in the EU on AWS Frankfurt and Cleura in Sweden, under ISO 27001 and 27701 certificates and a DPA. Favro has no built-in AI and charges no AI fees; an official MCP server lets Claude, ChatGPT or Cursor act on your behalf. Leaving means board-by-board exports or the API on Standard.
Caveat: The year marks the first dated app release found; Favro does not publish a launch date, user numbers or revenue.

Name: Fibery
Vendor: Fibery Limited. Privately held, venture-funded ($8.3 million to date); founded in 2016 by Targetprocess co-founder Michael Dubakov, remote team with offices in Warsaw and Nicosia.
Market_Evidence: Fibery reported 530 paid customers at the end of 2024 and 1.6 times as many in 2025, short of its 1,000-account goal, with a team of 30 (Fibery’s 2024 and 2025 year reviews; the latter published 21 January 2026).
Price_Note: Standard, per user per month billed annually; $15 billed monthly. Observers and guests are free.
Free_Plan_Note: Up to 10 users and 10 guests with 10 databases, unlimited entities, 1 GB of files, 250 automation runs a month and no AI credits; timeline, Gantt, whiteboard, feed, map, chart and dashboard views are private-only.
Plans: Free for up to 10 users; Standard $12 per user per month annually ($15 monthly); Pro $20 ($24 monthly); Enterprise $40 ($50 monthly) with a minimum of 25 paid users. AI credits come with each paid seat (250, 500 or 1,000 a month by plan), and Pro and Enterprise can buy extra usage at $15 per 1,000 credits.
Integrations_Note: Built-in synced integrations with 20+ tools including Jira (two-way on Pro and Enterprise), GitHub, GitLab, Slack, Zendesk, Intercom, HubSpot and Google Calendar, plus Zapier and Make; public REST and GraphQL APIs, a custom-integration SDK and an MCP server.
Hosting: AWS (EC2 and RDS). EU data residency on all plans; Enterprise can choose EU, US, UK or APAC. No self-managed or on-premise edition.
Security: SOC 2 Type II report from an independent auditor (on request); GDPR DPA; data encrypted in transit (TLS) and at rest. Google login on all plans, Microsoft login on paid plans; audit log kept 14 days on Free, 90 days on Standard, unlimited on Pro and Enterprise; SAML SSO, SCIM, IP restrictions and session settings on Enterprise.
Calendar_Sync: One way into Fibery: the Google Calendar integration syncs meetings, holidays and other events into an Events database shown in calendar views, and Pro and Enterprise can sync several email and calendar accounts per user. Fibery entities are not pushed to external calendars and no iCal feed is documented.
Data_Out: Export of the entire workspace as Markdown plus CSV on every plan; CSV import with field mapping; REST and GraphQL APIs, webhooks via automations, a custom-integration SDK and one-way Fibery-to-Fibery sync.
Platforms: Web, macOS and Windows desktop apps, iOS and Android apps (released 2026), and Chrome and Firefox extensions.
AI: Fibery AI (answers, data changes, workspace configuration, semantic search, transcription and highlight finding) on Standard, Pro and Enterprise, metered by 250, 500 or 1,000 monthly credits per paid seat, with paid overage on Pro and Enterprise; the Free plan has no AI credits. A remote MCP server on every plan serves Claude, ChatGPT and other agents. Fibery’s AI Terms (October 2026) state it does not use customer data to train third-party foundation models and contractually bars AI providers from training on inputs or outputs.
Value_for_money_Review: Ten free users with real databases, then $12 a seat; SSO needs the $40 Enterprise plan with 25 seats minimum.
Ease_of_use_Review: A blank workspace means designing databases, relations and views first; Fibery itself calls the people who do this Architects.
Enterprise_features_Review: SOC 2 Type II, audit logs and granular sharing, but SAML, SCIM and IP restrictions arrive only on Enterprise.
Interface_flexibility_Review: Custom databases and relations, formulas, ten view types, charts, whiteboards, JavaScript automations and AI-built custom apps.
Data_control_Review: EU hosting by default with SOC 2 Type II; US, UK or APAC residency only on the Enterprise plan.
Portability_Review: Any plan can export the whole workspace as Markdown and CSV, with REST and GraphQL APIs and CSV import.
Summary: Fibery is a configurable workspace in which a team defines its own databases (tasks, features, clients, objectives) and links them, then works on them through views, documents and automations. It suits product teams, agencies and start-ups that want one tool shaped to their process. Every database can be shown as a board, table, list, timeline with dependencies, Gantt, calendar, gallery, feed or map, with charts and dashboards over the data; whiteboards and collaborative documents link to entities. Rules, buttons and JavaScript scripts automate work. The cost of that freedom is set-up: nothing works until someone designs it, and time tracking is something you build. The free plan covers 10 users and 10 databases. Standard at $12 a seat (annual) adds unlimited databases, charts and whiteboards; Pro at $20 adds custom apps, advanced permissions, JavaScript automations and shared Gantt views; Enterprise at $40, from 25 seats, brings SAML, SCIM and regional hosting. Data is hosted on AWS in the EU unless an Enterprise customer chooses the US, UK or APAC, and Fibery holds a SOC 2 Type II report. Its AI terms forbid providers from training on inputs or outputs. Leaving is straightforward: a full Markdown and CSV export on every plan, plus REST and GraphQL APIs.
Caveat: Fibery is a small company (30 staff and 1.6 times as many paid accounts in 2025 as the 530 it had at the end of 2024, short of a 1,000 target). It set itself the goal of profitability in Q3 2026 and has published no update since, which matters for a tool you build your processes inside.

Name: Freedcamp
Vendor: Freedcamp Inc. Privately held and founder-led (Angel Grablev); based in Santa Barbara, California, United States.
Market_Evidence: Freedcamp’s homepage claims ‘millions of users’ (November 2026) and the company once reported 2 million; Latka estimates revenue near $770K and 7 employees (July 2025, third-party estimate).
Price_Note: Pro, per user per month billed annually; $2.49 billed monthly. Read-only and guest collaborators are free on paid plans.
Free_Plan_Note: Unlimited users, projects, tasks and storage (fair use) with 10MB files and the core apps; Gantt, custom fields, reports and backups need Business.
Plans: Free $0; Pro $1.49 per user per month annually ($2.49 monthly); Business $7.49 ($8.99 monthly); Enterprise $16.99 ($19.99 monthly), with volume discounts through sales.
Integrations_Note: First-party links to Google Drive, Dropbox, OneDrive, Slack, Google Calendar and email-in, plus Zapier for everything else. A public API is on every plan, and a hosted MCP server with 102 tools launched in 2026.
Hosting: AWS, US-based hosting per the privacy and Slack data-retention pages; no region named. Enterprise can buy an isolated private instance hosted by Freedcamp in an AWS region of the customer’s choosing for a fixed extra yearly fee.
Security: No SOC 2 or ISO certification of Freedcamp itself; the security page cites AWS’s ISO 27001, PCI and SOC reports, encryption in transit and at rest, and quarterly external audits. EU transfers under the Data Privacy Framework. 2FA from Pro; SAML SSO (beta) with Azure AD, Google, Okta on Enterprise; no SCIM or audit log published.
Calendar_Sync: GSync on paid plans pushes Freedcamp calendars to Google Calendar one way; any plan can share a calendar link to Google, Outlook or Apple, which refreshes on the client’s schedule. External calendars are not brought in.
Data_Out: Per-project XLS export of tasks, milestones, calendar, discussions, time and issues without comments or attachments; CSV Data Feed Links for tasks. Business (weekly) and Enterprise (daily) backups contain XLS, XML including comments, and attached files, kept for 30 days. Public API on all plans. Imports: tasks by XLS template only.
Platforms: Web, iOS, Android, Windows and macOS desktop apps, plus a separate Freedcamp Chat app for iOS and Android.
AI: AI usage allowances by plan (Free minimal, Pro limited, Business high, Enterprise near-unlimited with a top model); an AI project-creation assistant generates tasks and due dates, and a hosted MCP server opens the workspace to external AI clients. No published statement on model training with customer data was found.
Value_for_money_Review: Unlimited free users and projects, then $1.49 Pro; Gantt and custom fields need $7.49 Business.
Ease_of_use_Review: Each project switches on separate apps (tasks, time, wiki, CRM), which takes some setting up and learning.
Enterprise_features_Review: SAML SSO (beta) and white label on Enterprise, but no SCIM, audit log or certifications of its own.
Interface_flexibility_Review: List, Kanban, Gantt, calendar and table views with custom fields and statuses; dashboards only on Enterprise.
Data_control_Review: Runs on AWS in the US with no own certifications; Enterprise can buy a private instance in a chosen region.
Portability_Review: Per-project XLS exports skip comments; XML backups with files need Business; imports accept XLS tasks only.
Summary: Freedcamp is a long-running, low-cost project workspace from a small Californian company. It suits small businesses, schools and non-profits that want several teams in one place without per-seat bills, and offers discounts to education and non-profit users. A project bundles separate apps: tasks shown as a list, Kanban board or table, a calendar, milestones, time tracking, discussions, files and a password store. Business adds a Gantt chart with dependencies, critical path and slack time, plus a wiki, issue tracker, CRM, invoices, reports, custom fields and custom statuses. There is no general rules engine for automation; recurring tasks are the main exception. The free plan has no user or project cap, which is rare. Pro at $1.49 adds table view, subtasks, recurring tasks, Google Calendar push and cloud-file links, but most teams will want Business at $7.49 for the Gantt and custom fields. Guests and read-only collaborators cost nothing. Data sits on AWS in the US; Freedcamp cites AWS certifications rather than its own and handles EU transfers through the Data Privacy Framework. Leaving relies on per-app XLS exports, which omit comments, or Business backups in XLS and XML with attachments, plus the public API.
Caveat: Company size and AI data handling are not published; the user count is a homepage claim and revenue figures come from a third-party estimator.

Market_Evidence: Nifty’s homepage and integrations page (November 2026) say 20,000+ teams have been onboarded; no revenue, headcount or funding figures are published.

Calendar_Sync: Two-way Google Calendar and Outlook sync: tasks assigned to a user appear in a chosen external calendar with name, description and date changes kept in step, and external events appear in Nifty’s calendar.

Value_for_money_Review: Per-member Pro at $10 suits small teams, flat bundles get cheap past seven people, but Free stops at two projects.
Ease_of_use_Review: Each project opens on a familiar roadmap, task board and discussion, so small teams start quickly without configuration.
Enterprise_features_Review: SOC 2 and ISO 27001, Microsoft SSO from Business, but SAML only on Unlimited or Enterprise and no SCIM.
Interface_flexibility_Review: List, Kanban, swimlane, Gantt roadmap and calendar views, custom fields, automations, forms, docs and dashboards.
Data_control_Review: SOC 2 and ISO 27001:2022 on AWS, but no named region or residency choice.
Portability_Review: Importers for nine tools, but no documented workspace export, and the API needs the Business plan or above.
Summary: Nifty gathers a project’s milestones, tasks, documents, files and team chat in one workspace, with each project opening on a roadmap of milestones. It is aimed at agencies, product teams and small companies that work with clients. Projects combine a Gantt-style milestone roadmap with task lists, Kanban and swimlane boards, and team calendars. Tasks carry custom fields, dependencies, story points and timers. Portfolios, workloads, goals and automatic check-ins roll work up across projects, and clients join as guests. Orbit AI drafts documents and generates projects and tasks. Pricing comes in two forms: per-member plans (Pro $10, Business $16 billed annually) for small teams, and flat bundles (Pro $79 for 10 members, Business $124 for 30, Unlimited $399) for larger ones. The free plan admits unlimited members but only two active projects. Time tracking and custom fields start on Pro; the API and Microsoft SSO need Business. Data sits on AWS under SOC 2 and ISO 27001:2022 audits, with no region choice. Orbit AI sends content to OpenAI, which Nifty says may not train on it. Leaving is harder than arriving: importers cover nine tools, but there is no documented workspace export.
Caveat: Plans were re-cut in 2026 (plan IDs on the pricing page carry a 2026 suffix), and the choice between per-member and flat pricing changes the per-head cost sharply around seven people.

Name: Nozbe

Portability_Review: Task lists export to CSV, support sends a ZIP of everything, and the REST API and importers are on every plan.
Summary: Nozbe is a Polish task manager built around task-based communication: discussion happens in comments on tasks rather than in chat or email. It is sold to freelancers and small teams, with industry pages aimed at lawyers, estate agents and agencies. Work is organised as spaces, projects, sections and tasks, with an Incoming list for anything needing a person’s attention and a Priority list for their own day. A calendar view shows dated tasks, and AI can build a project from a description or a CSV file. There is no board, Gantt or custom field, and time tracking is manual fields only. The free plan covers three people and three projects. Premium is $9 per user per month (annual) for a single space; Business at $15 adds one subscription across spaces and unlimited admins. Per-user prices fall from ten users. Servers are at Hetzner in Germany, with backups and files on AWS in Paris and Frankfurt; a GDPR DPA is offered, but no certification or SSO. Nozbe AI uses Gemini; the vendor makes no statement on training. Task lists export to CSV, support will send a ZIP archive of all data, and a documented REST API makes leaving straightforward.
Caveat: Nozbe raised the prices of both Nozbe and Nozbe Classic from February 2026, after letting customers lock in the old rate until the end of January. The original Nozbe, now Nozbe Classic, still runs for existing users but gets no new features; this record covers the current Nozbe, formerly Nozbe Teams.

Summary: OmniFocus is the Omni Group’s task manager for people who run their lives by David Allen’s Getting Things Done. It is built for Mac, iPhone, iPad, Apple Watch and Vision Pro, and since 2019 the same database can also be reached from any browser. Actions sit in projects and folders, carry tags, due, planned and defer dates, and can be sequential so only the next step shows. Custom perspectives filter the whole database, and a weekly review keeps it current. There are no boards, calendar grid, Gantt, time tracking or sharing. OmniFocus for the Web is a companion: you must set up the database in an Apple app first, and it lacks the review, notifications and repeat editing. There is no free plan. The $99.99 annual subscription includes the Pro apps and web access. Owners of a $74.99 or $149.99 perpetual licence pay $49.99 a year more for the browser. For someone without an Apple device the web app is not usable on its own. Sync uses end-to-end encryption with a passphrase you choose, and the Apple apps can sync through your own WebDAV server instead of Omni’s, though the web app cannot. There are no published certifications. The Apple apps export CSV, HTML and plain text; AI is limited to on-device Apple Intelligence date parsing and Siri in beta.
Caveat: OmniFocus for the Web is not a standalone product: it needs a database first set up in an Apple app, and it lacks review, notifications and repeat editing.

Summary: Paymo began in 2007 inside a small web agency as a way to see where billable hours went, and it is still built around that loop: track time on tasks, then invoice the client. Time comes from in-app timers, desktop and mobile apps or the automatic Paymo Track, and feeds timesheets, estimates, invoices, expenses and profitability reports. Pro adds Gantt charts with dependencies, a portfolio Gantt, team scheduling with workload, timesheet approvals and leave planning. There is no AI and no workflow automation. The free plan is for one person with one client and two projects. Solo costs $5.90 a month billed annually for one user; teams need Plus at $10.90 per user billed annually ($15.90 monthly), which also unlocks integrations and the API, or Pro at $16.90 for scheduling and Gantt. Data is hosted on Amazon Web Services; Paymo publishes no certifications or region and offers no SAML SSO, though two-factor authentication and Google or Apple sign-in are available. The open REST API, with webhooks, covers all account data including comments and files, which makes a scripted exit realistic, while in-app exports are per report or table.
Caveat: A time-limited autumn 2026 offer for accounts created after 25 September 2026 bills monthly plans at the annual rate for the first three months; from month four Plus costs $15.90 per user.

Summary: Plaky is a board-based work tracker from CAKE.com, the company behind the Clockify time tracker. It is aimed at small and mid-sized teams wanting a cheap, monday.com-style tool, and is free for any number of users. Each board is a table of items with typed fields, viewable as a table, Kanban board, Gantt chart or pie and bar charts, with dashboards across boards and rule-based automations. The Gantt shows bars and subitems but no documented dependencies, and there is no calendar view or calendar sync. Time tracking works only by connecting a Clockify workspace. The free plan has no user cap but limits boards to 6 fields and keeps a 7-day activity log. Pro at $3.99 per seat (annual) adds Gantt, unlimited fields, private boards and 1,000 automation actions a month; Enterprise at $8.99 adds SSO, board permissions and an unlimited log. The $12.99 CAKE.com Bundle includes Clockify and Pumble. CAKE.com states ISO 27001:2022 and SOC 2 Type II at company level without naming the products covered, and says most processing is in the United States, with AWS, Microsoft and Hetzner as subprocessors; no Plaky data-region choice is documented. No AI features are listed. Leaving means per-board CSV exports, which omit comments, or the public API released in January 2026.
Caveat: Plaky’s Gantt has no documented dependencies and its time tracking requires a separate Clockify workspace, so teams needing scheduling or native timesheets will be paying for the bundle or another tool.

Summary: Productive is an operations system for agencies, consultancies and other professional services firms, joining project delivery to the money side: budgets, time, resourcing, invoicing and a sales pipeline. It suits firms of tens to hundreds of people that bill clients for time. Projects hold task lists with boards, lists, tables, a calendar of due dates, sprints and, from Professional, a Gantt layout with dependencies. Every task, time entry and booking hangs off a budget and a service, which is what makes profitability reports, forecasting and the Scenario Builder possible, and also what makes the first setup heavier than a task tool. Essential costs $10 per user per month billed annually ($12 monthly), with a three-seat minimum, and already includes time tracking, resource planning, expenses, docs, the API and an AI assistant with a monthly usage allowance. Professional at $25 adds the Gantt layout, approvals, rate cards and saved views; revenue forecasting, multiple subsidiaries, enforced SSO and webhooks are on Ultimate. Data sits on AWS in the EU under a SOC 2 Type II report and a DPA with Standard Contractual Clauses. AI runs on OpenAI, Anthropic and Google models, with a stated commitment that neither Productive nor its providers train on customer data. Exports are per table, so leaving at scale means the API.
Caveat: The Gantt layout and saved views sit on Professional, so a team that needs scheduling pays $25, not $10, per seat.

Security: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 certified; TLS for all traffic; continuous off-site backups. SAML SSO, Microsoft Entra External ID and IP allowlisting on Enterprise. No SOC 2, SCIM or audit log published.
Calendar_Sync: Free and Professional: one-way sync from Quire to Google Calendar (Professional adds Instant Sync). Premium and Enterprise: two-way Google Calendar sync and Google-to-Quire import. Apple Calendar sync is listed in the App Directory.

The API’s export endpoints (Professional and up) return JSON covering tasks, users, tags, sublists, documents, chats and dashboards, and CSV that can include text comments; attachments are not part of either. Imports: CSV, JSON from Asana, Trello and Todoist, and clipboard. Public REST API on all plans.

Value_for_money_Review: A free plan for 10 members and 4 projects, then $7.65 a member; two-way calendar sync needs $13.95 Premium.
Ease_of_use_Review: The nested list is quick to start with, though sublists, smart folders and views take some learning.
Enterprise_features_Review: SAML SSO and IP allowlisting on Enterprise only; no SCIM or audit log is published.
Interface_flexibility_Review: Nine views over one task tree plus custom fields, formulas, dashboards and approvals, but no rule-based automation.
Data_control_Review: ISO 27001:2022 certified, but all data sits on AWS in the United States with no region choice.
Portability_Review: CSV and JSON export on every plan, comments via the API export, importers for Asana, Trello and Todoist; attachments stay behind.
Summary: Quire is built around one idea: a task list that nests without limit, so a project breaks down into subtasks of subtasks and every other view reads from that tree. It is aimed at small teams and planners who think in outlines rather than boards. The same tasks appear as a nested list, a Kanban board, a timeline with finish-to-start dependencies, a calendar, a table, dashboards and insight charts. Sublists and smart folders slice work across projects, and collaborative documents sit beside the tasks. Time tracking, a Pomodoro timer and time reports arrive with Professional; timesheets and approvals with Premium. The free plan covers 10 members and 4 projects but stops at the list and board. Professional at $7.65 a member opens the timeline, calendar, table and time tracking, which is the tier most teams will need; Premium at $13.95 adds two-way Google Calendar sync. External guests count as paid members. Data is held on AWS in the United States under an ISO 27001:2022 certificate, and the privacy policy says it is processed in the US and Taiwan. Quire has no built-in AI assistant; instead an MCP server and CLI let outside AI tools read and write tasks. Exports in CSV and JSON plus a public API make leaving practical.
Caveat: Free-plan users get neither timeline nor calendar view, and external collaborators are billed as full members on paid plans.

Hosting: Amazon Web Services (S3 for files, RDS MySQL in a virtual private cloud); the region is not stated and there is no residency choice or self-managed edition.
Security: TLS 1.2, hashed and salted passwords, penetration testing; ISO 27001, PCI DSS Level 1 and SAS70 cited for the AWS data centre rather than Redbooth itself; SAML SSO (Okta, OneLogin, Shibboleth) on Pro and above; no SCIM or customer audit log documented. The security page still claims EU-U.S. and Swiss-U.S. Privacy Shield compliance (struck down in 2020) and its certification sentence names “Notion Inc.”; the DPA covers GDPR and CCPA but names no transfer mechanism.
Calendar_Sync: One-way iCal subscription per project or for all projects, showing all tasks or only yours, into Google, Outlook, Yahoo or Apple calendars; updates can take up to 24 hours. No two-way sync.
Data_Out: Organisation admins can export a ZIP of JSON files with all tasks including comments, task lists, conversations, notes, file links and workspaces; users can export their own data; Pro and Business can export all tasks to a spreadsheet (comments from the last 30 days); OAuth REST API; Gantt export.
Platforms: Web, iOS and Android, plus a Chrome extension and Gmail and Outlook add-ins.
AI: Redbooth AI (title trimming, subtask suggestions, comment summaries) on Business and Enterprise since June 2025; the MCP server for Claude and other assistants on Pro and Business. The AI provider and any training policy are not stated.
Value_for_money_Review: Free stops at two users; Pro at $9 a user adds dependencies, time tracking and SSO without a seat minimum.
Ease_of_use_Review: Workspaces, task lists and a board view that a new team can use the same day.
Enterprise_features_Review: SAML SSO from Pro and multi-organisation settings on Enterprise, but no SCIM, audit log or certification of its own.
Interface_flexibility_Review: Kanban, timeline, calendar and overview views with templates, web forms and reports; no custom fields or automation rules documented.
Data_control_Review: AWS hosting in an unnamed region with no residency choice, and a security page still citing Privacy Shield.
Portability_Review: Admins download every task, comment and conversation as JSON, plus an OAuth API, but importers are copy and paste.
Summary: Redbooth is a long-running team task manager, launched as Teambox in Barcelona and renamed in 2014. It is aimed at small and mid-sized teams such as agencies, construction firms and higher-education marketing groups that want tasks, discussion and video calls in one place. Work sits in workspaces holding task lists, conversations, notes and files. Tasks can be viewed on a Kanban board, a timeline with finish-to-start dependencies, a team calendar or a cross-workspace overview, and Zoom-powered HD meetings start from a task. Workspace templates, web forms and public links (added in October 2026) round it out; custom fields and built-in automation rules are not documented. The free plan stops at two users and two workspaces. Pro at $9 per user per month (annual) adds dependencies, time tracking, SAML SSO, video calls and the MCP server; Business at $15 adds reports, swimlanes, time estimates and Redbooth AI, which trims titles, suggests subtasks and summarises comment threads. Data is on AWS in a region the vendor does not name, with no residency choice; the security page still cites Privacy Shield, and neither the terms nor the DPA names a legal entity. The AI provider and training policy are not stated. Leaving is realistic: admins can generate a ZIP of JSON files with every task, comment and conversation.
Caveat: Redbooth is still sold and updated (web forms and public links in October 2026; iOS app 8.81 on 20 October 2026), but its terms and DPA name no legal entity or governing law, and its security page still relies on the Privacy Shield framework invalidated in 2020, with a sentence naming another company, Notion Inc.

Name: Shortcut
Vendor: Shortcut Software Company. Privately held, venture-backed (Battery Ventures, Greylock Partners); founded in New York City in 2014, headquartered there.
Market_Evidence: Shortcut says it is trusted by thousands of software teams (shortcut.com, November 2026); it raised about $39 million to its $25 million Series B in January 2020 and has around 80 employees (Wikipedia, 2026).
Price_Note: Team, per user per month billed annually; $10 billed monthly.
Free_Plan_Note: Up to 10 users, one team, one workspace, one workflow and 5 GB of storage, with boards, roadmap, iterations, docs and basic reports; no calendar feed or automations.
Plans: Free $0 for up to 10 users; Team $8.50 per user per month yearly ($10 monthly); Business $12 yearly ($16 monthly); Enterprise custom pricing. SAML SSO and SCIM are paid add-ons on Business and included on Enterprise; the Korey AI agent is billed separately from $99 per organisation per month.
Integrations_Note: The help-centre directory lists about 85 integrations, including GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Slack, Figma, Sentry, Zendesk, Zapier and coding agents through the hosted MCP server; a public REST API and outgoing webhooks on every plan.
Hosting: Amazon Web Services; the security page names no region and offers no data residency choice. No self-managed or on-premise edition.
Security: SOC 2 Type II (security, availability, confidentiality), reports available by request; a HIPAA BAA by request, which the security page offers on Business and Enterprise but the pricing table lists for Enterprise only; encrypted backups every 10 minutes. Google SSO on all plans; SAML SSO and SCIM (Okta only) are add-ons on Business and included on Enterprise; no customer-facing audit log is listed.
Calendar_Sync: Paid plans only: one-way public iCal feeds of due dates for your stories, the whole workspace, workflows, epics and objectives, for Google Calendar, Outlook or Apple Calendar; Google may take up to 12 hours to refresh, and nothing flows back.
Data_Out: CSV export of stories from a workspace, iteration, epic, label or space, including name, description, owners, labels, tasks and dates but not comments or attachments. REST API and outgoing webhooks; importers for Jira, Trello, Linear (with comments and files), Pivotal Tracker and CSV.
Platforms: Web application. No Shortcut app turned up in an Apple App Store search in November 2026, and neither the help centre nor the pricing page documents a mobile or desktop app; the iOS app announced in 2019 appears to be gone.
AI: Korey (launched September 2025) drafts specs, breaks them into stories, answers status questions and prepares work for coding agents; billed separately with 100 free interactions, then from $99 per organisation per month. Korey’s privacy policy says inputs and outputs are not used to train its models and its model providers are bound likewise. An MCP server is available on all plans.
Value_for_money_Review: Ten free users with sprints and a roadmap, then $8.50 a seat; custom fields and objectives wait for $12 Business.
Ease_of_use_Review: Stories, epics and iterations map directly onto how software teams already talk, and the board needs little setup.
Enterprise_features_Review: SAML and Okta-only SCIM are add-ons below Enterprise, there is no customer-facing audit log, and SOC 2 reports are by request.
Interface_flexibility_Review: Boards, backlog, roadmap table and timeline, docs, burndown and cycle-time reports and custom workflows, but no calendar view.
Data_control_Review: SOC 2 Type II and a HIPAA BAA, but one AWS hosting location with no residency choice and no self-managed edition.
Portability_Review: Story CSVs leave out comments, but the REST API is open on every plan and importers cover Jira, Trello, Linear and Pivotal.
Summary: Shortcut, called Clubhouse until 2021, organises software work as stories grouped into epics, timed into iterations and tied to objectives. It is sold to product and engineering teams that want sprints and a roadmap without Jira’s administration. Stories move across Kanban boards through custom workflows; a backlog, a roadmap with table and timeline layouts, built-in docs and reports for velocity, cycle time and cumulative flow sit alongside. The roadmap timeline draws no dependencies, there is no calendar view and no time tracking. Korey, an AI agent launched in September 2025, drafts specs and stories and hands work to coding agents. The free plan covers 10 users with one team and one workflow. Team at $8.50 a seat (yearly) adds automations, WIP limits, five workflows and the calendar feed; Business at $12 adds unlimited teams, objectives and key results, advanced custom fields and extra workspaces. SSO costs extra until Enterprise. Data sits on AWS with SOC 2 Type II audits and backups every 10 minutes; there is no region choice. Korey is priced per organisation, and Shortcut says Korey inputs and outputs are not used for training. Leaving means CSV story exports or the API, with importers in from Jira, Trello, Linear and Pivotal Tracker.
Caveat: SSO is a paid add-on below Enterprise and the AI agent Korey carries its own per-organisation subscription, so the per-seat price understates the cost for teams that want both.

Name: Sunsama
Vendor: Summay, Inc., a Delaware corporation with a business address in Alexandria, Virginia, US. Privately held and fully remote; Y Combinator backed in 2018, $2.4M seed, profitable since 2022.
Market_Evidence: No user count is published (the ‘300k+’ on its site counts newsletter readers); third-party profiles cite over 10,000 paying users and Latka estimates about $1.1M revenue for 2023, both unverified.
Price_Note: Pro, per person per month billed annually ($204 a year); $22 billed monthly. Each teammate in a shared workspace costs the same.
Free_Plan_Note: No free plan, and the vendor says it does not intend one; a 14-day trial with every feature and no card required.
Plans: Pro at $17 per person per month billed annually or $22 monthly, with unlimited integrations, AI, MCP and Zapier; Enterprise is quote-only and adds SSO/SAML, SCIM, audit logs and custom privacy terms.
Integrations_Note: Google, Outlook, iCloud and CalDAV calendars; Gmail and Outlook mail; Asana, ClickUp, GitHub, Jira, Linear, Monday.com, Notion, Todoist, Trello, Microsoft Planner and To Do, Slack, Teams, Toggl and Zapier. No public REST API or webhooks; a hosted MCP server is the only official programmatic route.
Hosting: Google Cloud Platform with MongoDB Atlas and AWS; ‘All data is stored in the United States.’ No EU residency, though the vendor says it could be considered for enterprise clients. No self-managed edition.
Security: SOC 2 Type I (September 2025) and Type II, report on request; ISO 27001 principles followed but not certified. TLS 1.2+ in transit and AES-256 at rest. SSO/SAML via WorkOS, SCIM and audit logs on Enterprise only.
Calendar_Sync: Two-way with Google, Outlook, iCloud and CalDAV (including Fastmail and Nextcloud) on Pro: events show in Sunsama, edits and timeboxed tasks write back to the source calendar.
Data_Out: Whole-history export from account settings (JSON per the security page); export data gained backlog and daily priority in October 2026, and users report subtasks are missing. No public REST API or webhooks; a hosted MCP server and Zapier can read and write tasks.
Platforms: Web, macOS, Windows, Linux, iOS and Android; the mobile apps are companions to the desktop planner.
AI: Sunny, a chat and voice assistant that creates and plans tasks, reads connected accounts and logs time, plus an OAuth MCP server for ChatGPT and Claude, both on Pro and out of beta in 2026. The privacy policy (updated 30 September 2026) says user data is never used to train models, including by third-party AI providers.
Value_for_money_Review: No free plan and $17 to $22 a month per person, more than most team tools charge for a single seat.
Ease_of_use_Review: A guided morning planning ritual and drag-to-calendar timeboxing; productive on day one if your work already lives in connected tools.
Enterprise_features_Review: SOC 2 Type II and SSO through WorkOS, but only on a quote-only Enterprise tier, with a thin billing-only admin role.
Interface_flexibility_Review: Day board, calendar panel, weekly objectives and channels, with an AI assistant; no custom fields, statuses or automation rules.
Data_control_Review: SOC 2 Type II and a GDPR DPA, but all data stays in the United States with no EU residency option.
Portability_Review: A full-history export exists, but there is no public API; only an MCP server and Zapier reach the data.
Summary: Sunsama is a daily planner for knowledge workers who want each morning to start with a deliberate plan. It is sold per person, with a shared-workspace option for teams who want one bill. The core object is a task placed on a day. A board of day columns sits beside your real calendar, and you drag tasks into time slots that write back to Google, Outlook or iCloud. Integrations pull issues, cards and emails in from Jira, Asana, Linear, Gmail and about 20 other tools. There are channels, weekly objectives and a timer, but no projects in the usual sense, no custom fields and no Gantt. There is one self-serve plan, Pro, at $17 a month billed annually or $22 monthly, and no free tier. That single plan replaced a short-lived split into Basic Pro and Power Pro in spring 2026, and it still makes Sunsama one of the dearest per-seat tools in this comparison for a single person. All data is stored in the United States on Google Cloud, MongoDB Atlas and AWS. SOC 2 Type II arrived in late 2025, and SSO, SCIM and audit logs sit on a quote-only Enterprise tier. The AI assistant, Sunny, and the MCP server are on Pro, and the privacy policy says customer data never trains models. Leaving relies on a whole-history export, since there is no public API.
Caveat: Pricing has changed three times in a year: $16 annually or $20 monthly in late 2025, Basic Pro at $20/$25 and Power Pro at $50/$65 by February 2026, then one Pro plan at $17/$22 by May 2026. The pricing FAQ kept quoting $20/$25 until late October 2026, which is where older third-party figures come from.

Name: Superlist
Vendor: Superlist GmbH, Germany, built by Christian Reber and the original Wunderlist team. Privately held and remote-first; venture backed by Cherry Ventures and EQT Ventures, with €13.5M raised by February 2024 (TechCrunch).
Market_Evidence: No user, customer or revenue figures are published (checked November 2026); €13.5M raised by February 2024 (TechCrunch) and third-party company profiles put headcount at 11 to 50, unverified.
Price_Note: Basic, per person per month billed annually ($59 a year); $6 billed monthly. Teams pay the same rate per member.
Free_Plan_Note: Free for ever with unlimited tasks and notes, but only five private and five shared lists, five people per shared list and 500MB of storage.
Plans: Free; Basic at $6 per person monthly or $59 a year; Super at $25 monthly or $249 a year, adding unlimited AI meeting notes, AI chat and summaries. Legacy Pro ($15 or $149) is closed to new buyers.
Integrations_Note: Gmail, Google Calendar, Slack, GitHub, Linear, Microsoft To Do and email forwarding, all on Basic. An MCP server (May 2026) lets AI assistants manage tasks; there is no public REST API or Zapier connector.
Hosting: Hetzner (Germany) is listed for infrastructure and hosting, with DigitalOcean, Cloudflare and Google Cloud as further processors; the policy does not state a data region. No region choice or self-managed edition.
Security: TLS encryption and general technical and organisational measures under GDPR, with a named data protection officer and a DPA on request. No SOC 2 or ISO 27001 claimed. No SSO, SCIM or audit log.
Calendar_Sync: Two-way with Google Calendar on Basic: dated tasks become all-day events (30-minute blocks with a time) and edits sync both ways; meetings show in Today. Outlook and iCloud are not supported.
Data_Out: Whole-account CSV export from Settings (January 2026); neither the January 2026 release note nor the help centre says whether comments or attachments are included. No public REST API; an MCP server can create and update tasks and lists. Data is deleted 30 days after termination.
Platforms: Web, macOS, iOS (iPhone and iPad) and Android; Windows users rely on the web app.
AI: Voice AI capture on Basic; AI meeting notes, AI chat, ‘Make’ content generation and email and Slack summaries on Super. Processors named are Google Gemini, OpenAI and Deepgram; the policy commits only that Google Workspace API data is not used to train general models.
Value_for_money_Review: A permanent free plan with five lists, then $5 a person annually for unlimited lists, sharing and integrations.
Ease_of_use_Review: Wunderlist-style lists with natural-language dates and voice capture; a new user is productive within minutes.
Enterprise_features_Review: Team billing and shared lists only: no SSO, admin console, audit log or published certifications.
Interface_flexibility_Review: Lists, sublists and rich task pages, but no board, calendar or custom fields, and only an MCP server for extension.
Data_control_Review: German company with a named DPO, a DPA on request and Hetzner hosting in Germany, but no certifications.
Portability_Review: Whole-account CSV export since January 2026, but no public API, and only Microsoft To Do sync as an importer.
Summary: Superlist is a to-do list app from the people who built Wunderlist, rebuilt after Microsoft closed that app. It is aimed at individuals and small groups who share household or project lists, with AI capture added on top. A list is a document: tasks sit beside text, headers and images, and each task opens into its own page of subtasks, notes and attachments. Lists can be shared with assignees and comments. Meeting notes and voice input turn speech into tasks. There is no board, calendar view, time tracking or Gantt. The free plan stops at five private and five shared lists. Basic, at $59 a year or $6 a month, removes those limits and opens the integrations, while Super at $249 a year is for heavy AI meeting-note use. Teams pay the same per-member rate. The privacy policy names Hetzner in Germany for hosting, alongside US processors, and Google Gemini, OpenAI and Deepgram for AI features; it does not say whether those providers may train on your data. A CSV export of the whole account arrived in January 2026, and an MCP server in May 2026, but there is no public API.
Caveat: Pricing was restructured in July 2025 and the free plan is capped at five lists; the vendor publishes no security certifications or user figures.

Name: TeamGantt
Vendor: TeamGantt. Bootstrapped and privately held, never taken outside equity; headquartered in Baltimore, Maryland, US, with a fully remote team of 22.
Market_Evidence: TeamGantt cites 2M+ users in 120 countries over its life, 20,000+ teams and a staff of 22 (teamgantt.com, about and pricing pages, November 2026).
Price_Note: Flat account pricing, not per user: Base is $589 a year (about $49.08 a month) or $59 billed monthly, for 1 manager, 10 collaborators and 5 projects.
Free_Plan_Note: TeamGantt Personal is free for 1 user, 1 project and 40 tasks with basic Gantt features and dependencies; anything shared needs a paid plan.
Plans: Personal free; Base $59 a month or $589 a year; Business from $120 a month or $1,140 a year with 5 projects, plus $24 a month per extra project up to 20; Builder Edition from $199 a month or $1,908 a year; Enterprise by quote.
Integrations_Note: Procore, Trello, Slack, Dropbox, Basecamp 2 and Zapier, plus an iCal feed and imports from MS Project, Primavera P6 and CSV; a public REST API with token auth and webhooks.
Hosting: Amazon Web Services; the privacy policy says personal information is stored in the United States. No region choice and no self-managed edition.
Security: SSL in transit, encrypted passwords, uploaded files served only through an authenticated script, two nightly backups. No SOC 2 or ISO 27001 published; SSO only on Enterprise.
Calendar_Sync: One-way iCal feed of your assigned tasks and milestones, or of selected projects, subscribed by URL in Google Calendar, Outlook or Apple Calendar; Google refreshes every few hours.
Data_Out: Export any project to CSV, PDF or Microsoft Project format on all paid plans. Public REST API (api.teamgantt.com/v1) covering projects, tasks, time blocks, comments, documents, custom fields and webhooks. Imports from MS Project .mpp, Primavera P6 and CSV.
Platforms: Web on Mac and PC; iOS and Android apps.
AI: AI project creation on all paid plans and a free AI Gantt chart maker on the website; the privacy policy names no AI provider and says nothing on training.
Value_for_money_Review: No per-seat bill, but Base caps at five projects and Business charges $24 a month for each project beyond five.
Ease_of_use_Review: Drag-and-drop bars and dependencies on one Gantt screen, and collaborators can only update progress, not reshape the plan.
Enterprise_features_Review: SSO only on the quoted Enterprise plan, no published certifications and a simple manager and collaborator model.
Interface_flexibility_Review: Gantt, list, calendar and Kanban views with workload and portfolio views; custom workflows only in Builder Edition.
Data_control_Review: US-only hosting on AWS, no certifications and a privacy policy that never mentions a DPA or AI.
Portability_Review: Any project exports to CSV, PDF or MS Project format, and the REST API reaches tasks, time, comments and documents.
Summary: TeamGantt is a Gantt chart scheduler that started in 2009 as a tool for a Baltimore roofing contractor, and it has gone back to those roots: its pages now speak mostly to home builders, remodelers and trade contractors, though any small team can use it. A project is a Gantt chart with groups, tasks, milestones and dependencies, with critical path on every plan; list and calendar views come everywhere, while Kanban, workload, time tracking, portfolios and advanced dependencies start at Business. Builder Edition adds lookahead schedules, material lead times and a Procore sync. Custom workflows are reserved for Builder Edition, and other automation runs through Zapier. Pricing is by account and project rather than seat. Base is $589 a year for 1 manager, 10 collaborators and 5 projects of up to 150 tasks; Business is $1,140 a year with unlimited people and 5 projects, then $24 a month per project up to 20. Trials need a card. Data is stored in the United States on AWS with nightly backups; TeamGantt publishes no certifications, no DPA and nothing on how its AI project creation handles data. Leaving is easier: each project exports to CSV, PDF or MS Project, and the REST API covers tasks, time, comments and files.
Caveat: Pricing is now a flat account fee with project caps (pricing page republished in September 2026), not the per-manager seats TeamGantt used to sell, so older comparisons quote the wrong model.

Calendar_Sync: None documented: no Google or Outlook sync and no iCal feed.
Data_Out: List views export visible columns to Excel or CSV; timesheets export with cost; Gantt downloads as PDF; a REST API (200 requests a minute per organisation) and webhooks read everything, including per-item history. A lapsed organisation is closed and cannot export until renewed.
Platforms: Web only; the vendor states there are no mobile apps.

Value_for_money_Review: No free plan and a three-licence minimum at $12, though API, AI chat and resource planning are all included.
Ease_of_use_Review: Configurable item types, fields and roles suit planners, but a new team has setup to do before it works.
Enterprise_features_Review: Custom roles, portfolio views and forced two-factor sign-in; SSO and SCIM only on quote-based Enterprise, and no own certification.
Interface_flexibility_Review: List, board, Gantt, schedule, mind map, timesheet and chart views with formula fields, templates and rollups, but no calendar.
Data_control_Review: EU Azure hosting by default, with Enterprise choices of Germany, US, dedicated, hybrid or on-premise installation.
Portability_Review: Excel and CSV export from list views and a full REST API, but a lapsed organisation cannot read its own data.
Summary: Teamhood is a project planning service from a Lithuanian company that now sells mainly to engineering, architecture and other technical firms running many projects with the same people. Its pitch is resource planning: showing each person’s planned hours across every project so overbooking is visible. Work is built from configurable item types and fields, shown in list, board, Gantt, schedule, mind map, timesheet and chart views. The Gantt reschedules dependent items, keeps baselines and previews what a change will move; the schedule view becomes a capacity plan when grouped by person. There is no calendar view, no calendar sync and no mobile app. The current product has one paid plan at $12 (€11) per user per month billed annually, with a three-licence minimum and guests counted as members. There is no free plan, only a one-month trial. Enterprise is quote-only. Customers of the earlier Teamhood Classic keep its separate four-plan structure. Data sits on Microsoft Azure in the EU; Enterprise can choose Germany or the US, or run dedicated, hybrid or on-premise installations. Teamhood holds no ISO 27001 or SOC 2 of its own. The Chat assistant uses OpenAI with stored responses off. List views export to Excel and CSV and the REST API reads everything, but only while the subscription is paid.
Caveat: Teamhood’s four-plan line-up (Personal, Team, Business, Enterprise) was renamed as recently as 3 December 2025; since then new customers get the rebuilt product on a single paid plan, while the earlier product, now Teamhood Classic, keeps those plans for existing customers. The vendor gives no switch date and no support timeline for Classic.

Summary: Toodledo is one of the oldest web task managers, built for people who want to slice a long task list by folder, context, goal, priority and length. It suits GTD-style planners who are comfortable with a spreadsheet-like screen. Tasks carry a long list of fields and can be sorted, filtered and saved as searches, with a Hotlist for what matters now. Beside tasks sit notes, hierarchical outlines, custom lists, habit tracking, a scheduler, an in-app calendar and a per-task timer. There is no board, timeline or rule automation, and collaboration is limited to sharing folders with named collaborators. The free plan stops at 10 folders, 30 items per list and a week of history, and leaves out subtasks and calendar sync. Standard at $3.99 a month billed annually removes most limits; Plus at $5.99 adds the scheduler, file uploads and up to 5 collaborators. Business is sold by quote. Data sits on US servers at Rackspace with nightly off-site backups; the vendor says only some data is encrypted at rest and publishes no certifications or AI features. Leaving is easy: a backup tool, several export formats and a free API cover the data.
Caveat: The privacy policy has not been updated since October 2018 and still refers to the EU-US Privacy Shield, which the EU Court of Justice struck down in 2020.

Summary: Tweek is a weekly planner that looks like a paper diary: seven columns, one per day, with tasks written straight into them. It suits individuals, couples and families who want a shared week rather than a project tool. Unfinished tasks roll over to the next day, ‘Someday’ columns hold undated items, and colour carries most of the organisation. Calendars can be shared with anyone or published as a web page. Month and day views, recurring tasks, reminders and subtasks are there; boards, projects, custom fields and time tracking are not. The free plan is generous for one calendar. Premium costs $49.99 a year or $5.99 a month and adds calendar sync, reminders, recurring tasks, subtasks, attachments and export, while Family at $89.99 a year covers five people. The vendor is Scada SIA in Riga, and data lives in Google Cloud Firestore with encryption at rest; the processor list places Google Cloud and DigitalOcean in the USA, and no certification is stated. An AI assistant described in the terms uses Anthropic’s Claude, with OpenAI for voice, and the terms say neither the providers nor Tweek train on your tasks. Export to CSV, XML, TXT or ICS and an open REST API make leaving easy.
Caveat: Tweek tasks never reach Google or Outlook calendars; only synced events can be edited from Tweek (Google fully, Outlook times since October 2026), so it does not work as a time-blocking tool.

Summary: Workflowy is a browser outliner in which everything, from a shopping list to a book draft, is a bullet that can hold more bullets. It suits individuals who think in nested lists and want notes and to-dos in one place. You zoom into any bullet to make it the page, tag and mirror items across the outline, and turn any branch into a board, table, to-do list or document. A daily calendar note collects dated items, and since 2026 a timeline and read-only Google Calendar import sit beside it. There is no time tracking, dependency chart or assignee field; @mentions do that job. The free plan has every feature but caps new content at 100 nodes a month, a limit a daily planner will meet quickly since each bullet counts. Pro costs $6.99 a month on an annual plan or $8.99 monthly, and Teams costs the same per user. AI chat, AI nodes and actions on Pro send content to OpenAI and Anthropic, which the AI terms say may not train on it. Exports to OPML and Markdown, Dropbox backup and a public API make leaving straightforward.

But the English blog has been silent since December 2024, no dated public changelog is readable, and the help centre still documents a Free plan the pricing page no longer offers, so confirm plan terms in the trial.

Name: Amazing Marvin
Vendor: Amazing GmbH, a Swiss company founded and run by Christina Willner. Privately held; the About page lists a team of three.
Market_Evidence: The homepage claims ‘5K+ happy users’ and the About page names three staff (both checked November 2026); no revenue or customer figures are published.
Price_Note: Marvin Pro, per person per month billed annually ($96 a year); $12 billed monthly. 50% student discount and ‘pay what you can’ on request.
Free_Plan_Note: No free plan: a 14-day trial without a card, after which data is kept but tasks cannot be added or completed until you subscribe.
Plans: One plan, Marvin Pro: $12 a month billed monthly or $96 a year ($8 a month) billed annually, with every feature included.
Integrations_Note: Calendar sync (Google, iCloud, Yahoo, CalDAV, Outlook in beta), Zapier, email-to-Marvin, a browser extension, Siri and Alexa; importers for Todoist, TickTick, Things, OmniFocus and CSV. A REST API with webhooks and direct database access is documented.
Hosting: Account data on Google App Engine and task data on IBM Cloudant, with transfers to the USA per the privacy policy (last updated 19 January 2020). No region choice; cloud sync can be disabled to keep data on the device only.
Security: Account data encrypted in transit and at rest, task data in transit (the help centre makes no at-rest claim for tasks), and optional two-factor authentication. No SOC 2 or ISO 27001 claimed. No SSO, SCIM or audit log.
Calendar_Sync: Two-way sync with Google, iCloud, Yahoo and CalDAV calendars on the single plan; Outlook and Exchange sync is in beta, and public ICS feeds can be imported read-only.
Data_Out: Backup of all data (tasks, projects, labels, time blocks, settings, notebooks, habits) as compressed or plain JSON; automatic backups in the desktop app; REST API, webhooks and direct CouchDB access. Projects can be copied out as text; no CSV export.
Platforms: Web, macOS, Windows, Linux, iOS, Android, Apple Watch and a browser extension.
AI: AI Braindump in the iOS and Android apps rebuilt in September 2026: typed or spoken text is sorted into tasks and projects, not yet on the web. The vendor names no AI provider and the January 2020 privacy policy does not mention AI or training.
Value_for_money_Review: No free plan, and $8 a month annually or $12 monthly is high for a one-person tool, though everything is included.
Ease_of_use_Review: Over 100 features and 300 settings switched on one by one; productive quickly only once you choose a workflow.
Enterprise_features_Review: A single-user tool by design: no admin console, no SSO, and only light task sharing and comments.
Interface_flexibility_Review: Lists, Kanban, calendar, smart lists, custom screens and dozens of toggled strategies, plus API and webhooks; no custom fields.
Data_control_Review: No certifications and a 2020 privacy policy naming US clouds, but cloud sync can be switched off to keep data local.
Portability_Review: Full JSON backup of tasks, projects and settings, a read-write API and many importers; no CSV export.
Summary: Amazing Marvin is a personal task manager and day planner that a Swiss micro-company has run since 2017. It is sold to individuals who struggle with procrastination or ADHD and want to tune the tool to how their own head works. Every feature is a ‘strategy’ you switch on or off: Kanban boards, a calendar with time blocking, time tracking, habits, goals, a task jar, reward points and procrastination prompts. The result can be a plain checklist or a dense personal system. There are no Gantt charts and no team workspaces; the only AI feature is a braindump sorter in the mobile apps. There is one plan, Marvin Pro, at $12 a month or $96 a year, with a 14-day trial and no free tier. Students get half price and the vendor offers pay-what-you-can on request, which is unusual. The mobile apps were rebuilt in September 2026. The privacy policy, last updated in January 2020, names Google App Engine and IBM Cloudant for storage, with US transfers; there are no certifications. Cloud sync can be turned off so data stays in the browser or desktop app. Backups export everything as JSON, and a documented API with webhooks and full database access makes leaving realistic.
Caveat: The privacy policy has not been updated since January 2020, so its hosting and transfer statements may not reflect current practice, and it says nothing about the AI braindump added to the mobile apps in September 2026.
